prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology and active forms of glucagon-like peptide-1 that made incretin-based therapies for diabetes and obesity possible

statement.case_for: All six of us placed B041 first, but unanimity of opening rank is not the argument. The argument is that this is a discovery with a discernible change in the field: GLP-1 was shown to be a physiological incretin and gut-brain signal, its active (7-36) form was identified and characterised, and that knowledge is what turned a labile peptide into a drug class. The effect on diabetes and obesity care, with cardiovascular and renal benefit in large independent trials, is established and still growing. A prize to Holst (incretin physiology and secretion of active GLP-1), Drucker (GLP-1 biology and actions) and Mojsov (identification of the active peptide form) rewards the discovery rather than the product, which fits the principle that the prize recognises a specific discovery. The decades of independent confirmation also answer any maturity concern.
statement.case_against: The weakest point is attribution. Credit is spread over proglucagon processing, peptide chemistry, physiology and industrial analogue design, and a three-person limit forces us to leave out Lotte Bjerre Knudsen, whose long-acting analogue work is decisive for the drugs patients actually take, as well as figures outside the supplied names such as Habener. Mojsov's priority for the active form is also contested in the literature, and I cannot verify those details from the files. If the committee reads the discovery as the drug rather than the physiology, the trio is the wrong trio. A second concern is that a prize this heavily weighted to translational success could look like a prize for commercial impact.

responses.point: Basic physiology and peptide identification are best captured by Drucker, Holst and Mojsov, but Knudsen is the key figure for the long-acting drugs and could displace one name if translation is emphasised.
responses.response: I agree with the framing and would keep the physiology trio. Displacing Mojsov for Knudsen would turn the citation into a drug-development prize, and the scientific insight that made those drugs conceivable would then rest on a smaller base. I would only reopen the question if the committee agreed that the citation should centre on the therapies, in which case I would want to argue explicitly about which of the three is least central, not assume it is Mojsov. I do not think Knudsen's exclusion is free of cost, and I would not hide it.

responses.point: TOR and mTOR (B011) is a foundational growth-control pathway, ranked third, with Hall and Schreiber as the core and Sabatini best avoided because of uncertainty about his record.
responses.response: I accept that the TOR pathway is conceptually foundational and extensively validated, and I ranked it seventh with Hall and Schreiber as well. My reservation is attribution: the steps from TOR genetics in yeast, to rapamycin target identification, to mammalian mTOR complexes are contested between several groups, so a clean citation is hard to write. I would not exclude Sabatini only on the basis of an unverified concern about his record; that is not something I can assess from the evidence we hold, and the scientific question of his contribution should be argued separately. I do not place B011 ahead of CAR-T or BCR-ABL, where both attribution and downstream confirmation are firmer.

responses.point: Optogenetics (B039) is methodologically transformative with very broad adoption, and Deisseroth, Nagel and Hegemann is one reasonable configuration.
responses.response: I do not dispute the value of optogenetics as a tool, and I note that you also cautioned against letting field familiarity colour the ranking. My difficulty is that the discovery spans channelrhodopsin characterisation (Nagel, Hegemann, Bamberg), neuronal deployment (Boyden, Deisseroth) and earlier genetically targeted light control (Miesenboeck). Six credited names against a limit of three means any trio omits someone with a strong claim, notably Bamberg and Boyden. It is also a research method whose clinical effect is still early, whereas I weigh a clear change in the field for medicine. I would put it behind B030 and B023, but I would not rule it out as a second part of a two-part prize.

responses.point: The unfolded protein response (B035) is a clean two-person allocation (Mori, Walter) for a fundamental quality-control principle that remains unprized.
responses.response: I agree it is the cleanest allocation on the list, and that Mori and Walter fit the discovery well. My reservation is the same one I raised in my own ballot: the basic mechanism is mature, but the translational thread (integrated stress response, ISRIB) is a separate and still-developing line, so I would keep the citation strictly mechanistic. I rank it fourth, below the two clinically proven alternatives, mainly because the committee has stronger medical evidence for B030 and B023, not because I think the science is weaker. As a second part sharing the prize it is credible, but it would push the union past three names given my preferred trio, so I would not combine them.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept a three-person physiology trio that excludes Lotte Bjerre Knudsen, or will prefer to substitute her for one of the three.
The extent of Mojsov's priority for the active GLP-1(7-36) form relative to other early workers, which I cannot verify from the files.
Whether the choice among B030, B023 and the mechanistic candidates is better made on clinical maturity or on conceptual originality.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict specific to B041 or the other shortlisted candidates is apparent from my profile. For transparency, my profile records past nuclear-receptor co-authorship with Ronald Evans (not a credited name on the shortlist), about twenty co-authored works with Per Svenningsson and one with Abdel El Manira (2009); none of these bears on a shortlisted candidate. As Secretary I also note that my voting status is not stated in the profile.
